title: Supercharge breaks Rommel

facts.text: At 1:05 a.m. on 2 November 1942, the British Eighth Army under General Bernard Montgomery launched Operation Supercharge, its final push to break Rommel's line at El Alamein.

The attack was run by Lieutenant General Bernard Freyberg's 2nd New Zealand Division, but most of the assault infantry were British: the 151st (Durham) Brigade and the 152nd (Highland) Brigade, joined by the New Zealand 28th (Maori) Battalion.
The infantry moved off in the dark behind a creeping barrage from about 360 guns, after hours of bombing by the Royal Air Force.
The plan was to punch a corridor about 4,000 yards deep, so British tanks could cross the Rahman track and reach Tel el Aqqaqir, the heart of the Axis defense.
The two British brigades reached their objectives before dawn, between about 3:45 and 6 a.m.
Next, the 9th Armoured Brigade under Brigadier John Currie had to charge straight at a screen of German and Italian antitank guns, including deadly 88 mm guns, along the Rahman track.
Currie warned that his brigade could lose half its strength. Freyberg told him Montgomery had "accepted the possibility of losing 100% casualties" to make the break.
The tanks went in at 6:15 a.m., half an hour late, with the sun rising behind them and lighting them up for the enemy gunners.
The brigade began the attack with 94 tanks. By the end, fewer than 25 were still running, and 230 of its men were killed, wounded or missing. It smashed many guns but did not open the gap.
Afterward a New Zealand brigadier found Currie resting on a stretcher and asked where his tanks were. Currie pointed to the handful around him: "These are my regiments."

British 1st Armoured Division tanks then came forward, and Rommel threw his panzers and the Italian Littorio Division at them near Tel el Aqqaqir. The counterattack failed, and the Afrika Korps lost about 70 tanks that day.
That night the Afrika Korps commander reported he would have at most 35 tanks the next day. Rommel decided to fall back to Fuka and warned his superiors of the "gradual destruction" of his army.
What came next: on 3 November Hitler ordered Rommel to stand fast, but on 4 November the British broke through and the Axis army began its long retreat west.

photoNote: Soldiers look over a knocked out German 88 mm gun in its pit near Tel el Aqqaqir, November 1942. Australian War Memorial 040977, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons. Small file (640 px wide), so it may look soft on the card. Backups if a sharper one is wanted: IWM E 18869, a Priest self propelled gun of 1st Armoured Division readied on 2 November 1942; IWM E 18839, an 88 mm shell hole in a Churchill tank turret, 2 November 1942. No photo of Currie or of the 2 November barrage was found; the well known barrage photo (IWM E 18465) is from 23 October and was used for No. 013's story.

film.file: Source Film folder (the 480p copy used for Nos. 021 and 024; also No. 037)
film.shot_notes: Use the film's Supercharge section, the final night attack and the dawn armored fighting before the breakout: infantry moving up in the dark behind the barrage, tanks advancing at first light, antitank guns in action. Do not reuse No. 013's barrage clip (29:21 to 29:24 and 27:07 to 27:20), No. 021's Kidney Ridge shots (35:15 to 35:50) or No. 024's air attack shots (40:41 to 41:39), and keep the breakthrough, prisoner and pursuit shots for No. 037 on Wednesday. Leave out staged close ups, captured enemy newsreel, and any stretch with music or narration under it. Keep the film's own battle sound if a clean stretch exists.

film.date_note: Desert Victory does not date each shot; if the chosen shots are not clearly from 2 November, the caption should say the film shows the final days of the Alamein battle.
